business_problem: FoodLogiQ needed a faster, better-managed data platform for millions of daily food-chain records because its previous database setup was slow, costly, and hard for a small team to operate and optimize.
solution_summary: FoodLogiQ moved its food-chain data platform onto MongoDB Atlas on AWS after struggling with slow clusters, poor query patterns, and earlier attempts to use MongoDB in a relational way. Atlas gave the company a managed document database that fit its small operations team while Justin LaBreck and MongoDB guided a deeper cleanup of development practices, query design, indexes, and cluster management. The team now validates query performance before changes reach customers, traces data sources more easily, and uses Atlas automation to create production clones without lengthy manual checks. Atlas also simplified future multi-cloud continuity conversations because node counts and regional placements can be adjusted without rebuilding the architecture around the food traceability application.

solution_components.name: MongoDB Atlas
solution_components.role: Runs FoodLogiQ's managed cloud document database on AWS and automates operational tasks such as scaling, cloning, and issue resolution.

data_flow: Food supply chain records and application data are stored in MongoDB Atlas on AWS, developers tune queries and indexes against that live dataset, and Atlas clones and multi-cloud node placements support customer analytics, continuity, and operational troubleshooting.
business_outcome: FoodLogiQ cut clone times from a day to half an hour, halved hosting bills, improved query and index discipline, and gave its small team a more scalable foundation for enterprise continuity and future growth.
